name: Broad-spectrum sunscreen

lead: Broad-spectrum sunscreen is a topical product with filters that block both UVB and UVA radiation, sold as lotions, gels, sticks and sprays. It is the central anti-ageing product in skincare circles: it limits the sun-driven wrinkles, dark spots and tone changes, and keeps acne marks from darkening.

Filters either absorb UV (chemical) or reflect and scatter it (mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide), reducing the dose that reaches skin. In the Nambour randomized trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen users had about 24 percent less skin ageing over 4.5 years than discretionary users. Daily sunscreen is a standard dermatology recommendation.

paras: Users apply it every morning to the face and exposed skin and reapply during the day when outdoors. Chemical, mineral and hybrid formulas are chosen by feel, finish and white cast.

Protection depends on applying enough and reapplying, and most people under-apply. Irritation and allergic reactions occur, and mineral products can leave a white cast. Reviews note open questions on systemic absorption of some chemical filters and debate over environmental effects.

web.title: Sunscreen: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun (FDA)

angle.text: Blocking UVA and UVB cuts the photoageing that shows up as wrinkles, dark spots and uneven tone, so your skin looks younger for longer. Photoprotection is well studied; chemical-versus-mineral debates are mostly about feel and white cast.

lead: Broad-spectrum sunscreen is a topical product containing filters that absorb or block both ultraviolet B (UVB) and ultraviolet A (UVA) radiation. It is the everyday tool people use to keep skin looking younger and more even: ultraviolet exposure is a major driver of wrinkles, rough texture, uneven pigment, visible small vessels and loss of firmness, and a product that reduces the dose reaching the skin is used to slow those changes on the face, neck and hands. [1][2][3]

Products come as lotions, creams, gels, sticks, powders and sprays, and their filters are grouped as chemical (organic molecules that absorb UV), mineral (zinc oxide and titanium dioxide) or hybrid. A rating such as SPF describes protection against sunburn-producing UVB, while the phrase "broad spectrum" signals that UVA protection has also been tested. [1][4][5]

Dermatology bodies recommend regular broad-spectrum sunscreen use for preventing sunburn, skin cancer and photoaging. A 2013 randomized trial in Nambour, Australia, found less skin aging in daily sunscreen users than in discretionary users, and a 2021 review concluded that evidence supports sunscreen for photoaging, dyspigmentation, DNA damage and photocarcinogenesis. [6][7][8] Research and commentary also describe practical limits such as how much product people actually apply, the small number of approved filters covering long-wave UVA, questions about systemic absorption of some chemical filters, and debate about environmental effects. [1][2][9][10]

In looksmaxxing and skincare communities, daily sunscreen is treated as a foundation of "skinmaxxing" and a low-cost anti-aging step, and much discussion concerns white cast, tints, texture under makeup and the differences between filters sold in different countries. [11][12][13]

paras: Chemical sunscreens use organic molecules, many of them aromatic compounds conjugated with carbonyl groups, that absorb UV energy and release it as heat; avobenzone is a widely used UVA filter that degrades in light unless stabilised by other ingredients. Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, which mainly absorb UV and also reflect and scatter some of it. Hybrid products combine both types. [1][14]

Ultraviolet radiation damages skin through different routes. UVB penetrates mainly the epidermis and is the principal cause of sunburn and a primary mutagen. UVA reaches deeper into the dermis, where it is described as damaging collagen, elastin and the extracellular matrix and generating reactive oxygen species. Wikipedia's photoaging article describes UV activating signalling pathways that raise matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that break down collagen, while collagen synthesis falls in photoaged skin. [3] Early experiments in hairless mice reported connective-tissue damage after months of UVA exposure alone. [15]

SPF is the ratio describing how much of the burning radiation reaches the skin compared with unprotected skin, measured at a standard application density of 2 mg per square centimetre. By that definition SPF 15 lets about one fifteenth of burning radiation through, SPF 30 about one thirtieth and SPF 50 about one fiftieth, so the share blocked rises from roughly 93 percent to 97 and 98 percent. In the United States the test is done on volunteers under artificial sunlight; laboratory spectrometer methods are also used elsewhere. [4]

Because SPF mainly reflects UVB, several systems rate UVA separately: the in vitro and in vivo PPD (persistent pigment darkening) method, the EU UVA seal requiring UVA protection of at least one third of the SPF, the Boots star system in the UK and Ireland (three to five stars), and the PA system used in Japan and on many Asian products, to which PA++++ was added in 2013 for a PPD of 16 or higher. [1] US rules effective from 2012 define "broad spectrum" as UVA protection proportional to UVB protection under a standardised test. [1]

A 2021 review notes that few FDA-approved filters protect against long-wavelength UVA above about 370 nm and none protect against visible light, and that antioxidants and DNA-repair enzymes such as photolyase have been proposed as additives for aspects of photoaging. [7]

The SPF on a label comes from testing at 2 mg per square centimetre, which Wikipedia puts at roughly 35 ml (about an ounce) for an average adult body and about a quarter to a third of a teaspoon for the face. Studies cited there found that people typically apply a quarter to a half of the tested amount, and that the resulting protection may be closer to the fourth root or square root of the labelled value. [1][4]

FDA consumer guidance says SPF is not a multiplier of time in the sun, advises applying before going outdoors and reapplying at least every two hours and after swimming or sweating, and notes that "waterproof" claims are not allowed: products may only be labelled water resistant for 40 or 80 minutes. Products that are not broad spectrum or have SPF below 15 must carry a warning that they protect against sunburn but not skin cancer or early skin aging. The agency advises not spraying sunscreen directly onto the face and treating products as expired three years after purchase if no date is printed. [5]

In practice, people using sunscreen for appearance describe facial formulas worn under moisturiser or makeup, tinted mineral products, light gels and sticks for reapplication, and hats or clothing as complements. Tinted products containing iron oxides are discussed because iron oxides reflect visible light, which is relevant to pigmentation concerns, and a looksmax.org reply in one thread notes that zinc oxide, titanium dioxide and Tinosorb M can leave a white cast while iron oxides can add a darkening tint. [11]

Wikipedia records ancient plant-based skin protection including olive oil among the Greeks, extracts of rice, jasmine and lupine in Egypt, thanaka paste in Myanmar, borak paste among the Sama-Bajau and masonjoany in Madagascar from the 18th century. [1]

Scientific understanding followed in steps: Sir Everard Home suggested in 1820 that something other than the sun's heat caused sunburn, Erik Johan Widmark experimentally linked UV to skin burns in 1889, and Hausser and Vahle identified 297 nm as the wavelength responsible for sunburn in 1921. [1]

Commercial products appeared in the 1930s. Australian chemist H.A. Milton Blake released a sunscreen containing 10 percent tannic acid in 1932, and IG Farben chemists patented novantisolic acid, marketed as Delial, in 1933 to 1936. L'Oreal released its first sunscreen in 1936. Benjamin Green created Red Vet Pet for US military personnel in the Pacific in 1944, and Coppertone and Bain de Soleil commercialised similar products in the early 1950s. [1]

Franz Greiter introduced Gletscher Creme in 1946, the basis for Piz Buin; it is estimated to have had an SPF of about 2. Wikipedia credits Greiter with introducing the SPF rating in 1974, adapting earlier calculations by Friedrich Ellinger and Rudolf Schulze, and water-resistant sunscreens were introduced in 1977. [1][4]

The United States regulates sunscreen as an over-the-counter drug, whereas the EU and Japan treat it as a cosmetic, which Wikipedia notes results in fewer approved filters in the US. The FDA's 2011 rules, taking effect in 2012 and 2013, defined "broad spectrum" and the labelling of SPF; the Sunscreen Innovation Act of 2014 was passed to speed approvals of new filters; in 2019 the FDA proposed to classify filters and to prohibit labels above SPF 60; and by 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classified as generally recognised as safe and effective, while PABA and trolamine salicylate were removed from the monograph over safety concerns. [1][4]

In June 2026 the FDA added bemotrizinol as a permitted active ingredient, described by Wikipedia as the first new sunscreen ingredient approved in about 20 years, and the FDA's consumer page records the change. [1][5]

Elsewhere, the EU requires a minimum SPF of 6, a UVA to UVB ratio of at least one third and a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm, caps labels at SPF 50+, and requires nanoparticles to be disclosed. Australia raised its label limit from 30+ to 50+ in 2012; Japan's SPF scale runs from 2 to 50 with PA ratings for UVA; China requires animal safety testing before approval; and the Mercosur countries began regulating in 2012 with a longer list of approved ingredients than the US or EU. [1][4] FDA guidance warns that products sold outside the United States may differ from US products. [5]
Human research on sunscreen is extensive, spanning trials of photoaging, actinic keratoses, melanoma, naevi and vitamin D, as well as safety studies of absorption.

The Nambour trial in Queensland, Australia, compared daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use with discretionary use, and beta-carotene with placebo, for effects on skin aging. A trial summary reports about 24 percent less aging over 4.5 years in daily users among 903 adults, and Wikipedia describes the daily users as having smoother, more resilient skin. [6][8][1] A 2021 review concluded that evidence supports sunscreen in preventing photoaging, dyspigmentation, DNA damage and photocarcinogenesis. [7]

A 1993 randomized trial in the New England Journal of Medicine tested daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on solar keratoses, a precursor of squamous-cell carcinoma. [16] A 2011 follow-up of a randomized trial reported reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use. [17] Wikipedia states that sunscreen helps prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, with weaker evidence for basal cell carcinoma. [1]

A 2018 meta-analysis of 29 studies with 313,717 participants, mostly case-control, found no significant association between sunscreen use and skin cancer overall (odds ratio 1.08, 95 percent CI 0.91 to 1.28), for melanoma (1.10) or for non-melanoma skin cancer (0.99). Cumulative evidence before the 1980s showed a positive association with melanoma, which declined over time, and the analysis had very high heterogeneity; the authors attributed the findings partly to study design problems and earlier-era products. [18] A 2025 review summarises sunscreen in skin cancer prevention. [19]
A randomized trial in white children examined broad-spectrum sunscreen use and the development of new naevi (moles). [20]

Wikipedia notes that even moderate sunscreen use can substantially reduce vitamin D synthesis under laboratory conditions, with diet and supplements as alternatives. [1] An international expert panel review in 2019 concluded that broad-spectrum sunscreens that prevent erythema are unlikely to compromise vitamin D status in healthy populations, and a 1995 randomized trial in Australia examined regular use and vitamin D levels. [21][22]

Two randomized clinical trials published in JAMA in 2019 and 2020 measured plasma concentrations after sunscreen application in healthy volunteers, including avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate; the 2020 abstract states the aim of determining how quickly exposure exceeds the 0.5 ng/mL threshold recommended by the FDA. Grokipedia reports that concentrations exceeded that threshold and that no harm has been shown. [9][10][14] Wikipedia states that the FDA has not concluded that the organic filters in question are unsafe. [4]

Allergic and irritant contact dermatitis can occur to filters or other ingredients; Wikipedia lists oxybenzone and cinnamates as allergens. [1] Aerosol products drew attention when the laboratory Valisure reported benzene in about 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens it tested, traced to propellant impurities and followed by voluntary recalls. [1][4]

Environmental concerns have led to local restrictions: Hawaii banned sales of products containing oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018, Palau banned ten ingredients in 2020, and Key West, the US Virgin Islands and Bonaire have also restricted some. Wikipedia reports measurements of oxybenzone in Hawaiian bays above levels considered toxic to corals, and that "reef-safe" labels are unregulated and have no agreed definition. Environmental advocates favour mineral filters as a precaution, while Wikipedia reports that public health bodies' consensus is that the risk of sun-induced skin cancer outweighs unproven toxicity concerns. [1]

FDA guidance advises against sunscreen for infants under six months without consulting a doctor, and clinical literature covers use in pregnancy. [5][23] A review of sunscreen myths addresses higher SPF, use in darker skin types and vitamin D. [24]

Daily sunscreen is a staple of appearance-community skincare advice and is framed as the main protective measure against photoaging, often paired with retinoids, vitamin C and moisturiser in routines. A looksmax.org guide thread describes sunscreen as cheap anti-aging, cites the Nambour result and the claim that most skin aging is sun-driven, and lists the benefits of sun exposure such as vitamin D. [12]

Frequent topics are cosmetic: one member with light skin and a warm undertone reported that mineral sunscreens either left a white cast or made the skin look darker, and replies discussed filters and iron oxides. [11] Another thread discusses regional products, with a poster stating that European and Asian sunscreens use filters not allowed in the United States. [13] A further thread asks whether sunscreen is harmful. [25] Published research summarised above supports an effect on measured photoaging, while its authors and reviewers also describe limits such as application amount.

lore.intro: Daily sunscreen is widely promoted on looksmax.org as a cheap anti-aging step, alongside discussion of white cast, ingredient safety and differences between regional filters. [11][12][13]

claims.claim: Daily sunscreen is the most cost-efficient anti-aging measure and slows skin aging.
Most skin aging, roughly 90 percent, is caused by the sun.
Sunscreen chemicals are toxic, so hats are preferable.
Mineral sunscreens leave a white cast or darken the skin, and European or Asian filters are better.
Sun exposure benefits, such as vitamin D and higher testosterone, argue against heavy sunscreen use.
Mineral or tinted sunscreens with iron oxides protect against pigmentation triggered by visible light.
Higher SPF numbers give proportionally more protection, so SPF 100 is twice as good as SPF 50.
